text:
Remotion is slow and indirectly causes "slop" videos. I switched to fframes, render time of my vid I attached here went from 700 seconds to <21 seconds. I used fframes to create variants of scenes and iterated obsessively on the little details over and over again, which add up fast to create a "non-slop" video.

As you scale number of variants across many scenes, your time spent rendering grows quickly! fframes literally renders my vid faster than it plays.

I created a skill to create iterations of scenes. I focsued on iterating on both scene design and sound design. Letting sound design lead the scene works well with fframes as cohesive scene <> sound development necessitates experimentation. 

Using Astra/Sol/Opus subagents to look up examples beforehand for inspiration is a great way to get unique variants. Make sure to tell them both what you like and what you hate (!) about what they make to instill direction.

Rendering a scene of ~120 frames, or 2 seconds at 60 fps video, sped up by 20x when I switched to fframes from Remotion.

Search tools for agents are nearly instant and have opened up doors to deep research. Jev made decision models cheap and we started deciding on unique things. We must make sure our primitives for video creation are as fast, if not faster, to allow for multi-agent scaling of intelligence for creative exploration, or in our case video iteration. 

This entire vid was made only with fframes.

text:
Remotion really changed the game...  

These AI animations are just insane.  

But most people don't know how to create them

In these 33 mins, you'll learn everything you need to know Claude Code video editing https://t.co/6v6hixtAz4

I don’t ask Claude to “make a video” anymore

I give it 6 small jobs. each one produces one file, and the next job starts from that file

> reference  spec.md
it watches a video I like and writes down why it works: pacing, first motion, cut rhythm

> data  data.json
it pulls the real numbers and keeps the source next to every figure

> story  story.md
one point, one hero number, three beats. before anything moves

> motion  Scene.tsx
it writes every frame as code with Remotion and a motion-design skill

> direct  timing.ts
I give notes in plain words. “title is a beat late”  one line changes

ship  final.mp4
it renders stills, checks them against the spec and the data, then waits for my approval

why small jobs work better:

each step has one clear output, so it’s easy to check
if something looks off, you know exactly which file to fix
nothing gets re-rolled, so the rest of the video stays the same

one big prompt gives you a guess
six small jobs give you a video you can actually edit

full setup, prompt and the 10 open-source skills are in the article

I made this product launch video over the weekend with just prompts

It's all vibe coded

https://t.co/V9i8Z6N8ow

There's something you should know, though:

Like everyone else, a few days ago my timeline started getting full of videos like this when Remotion launched their Claude skill, so I decided to give it a go

I was captivated by all the examples, so I started like everyone was saying: "just write a prompt"

I typed the prompt, and it created an extremely bland, untasteful, stock-looking video

10 prompts in and it was not getting better. It was very, very bland. But at least it was something, so I kept going at it

I ended up spending my entire weekend on this, 2-3 days of work. Only to realize my original reference videos that inspired me to get started were all fake

Everyone was outright lying about their results. They all claimed "I made this with just one prompt", but it was just bait, they didn't really use Remotion or code at all, it was just a normal, human-made motion video

Then you expand the X post and read the replies and they're all like "haha joke" in the comments, but their main post already got 1.5 million views and bamboozled everyone who didn't read further

And this is a problem: when a viral trend happens, these posts flood your timeline, and you only realize that they're all noise and bait (and that they haven't even used the tools they claim) when you click through the post and read its comments. But 90% of people (like me, initially) just see the post on their timeline while scrolling, and assume it's all real. You don't go in to check every single post you see: you just like it, or save it for later, and carry on with your day, thinking what you saw was the real thing, and that it's all outstanding results, and that motion designers are really done

And it's so anxiety inducing, because everyone is hyping their results, but most of it is just not true. I have stopped reading X lately because going in makes me so anxious, everyone is claiming extraordinary outlier results just for the views and clicks, and you feel like you're lagging behind and you're not good enough because you don't get those results

So for this video I decided to actually take the tech out for a spin, and see what results I could really get out of it

I used Remotion and Claude Code 4.5, but contrary to what everyone was claiming, this video was not "just a prompt". It was fully vibe coded, but it required much more than a prompt. It was multiple days worth of work

Here's what I learned:

- Making vibe coded videos with Remotion is ~10-20x slower than building app code. I've been wasting my Claude limits on this video

- Everything takes a lot of manual work and reprompting. You often need to go frame by frame correcting tiny things

- It makes very silly mistakes

- Even Opus 4.5 has very very limited knowledge of spatial / visual things. It doesn't understand well z-indexes, layers, compositions, proportions, temporal coherence, etc. Claude Code feels extremely dumb when creating code for Remotion videos, which surprised me a lot, beacuse I had been mind blown by how incredibly well it worked with my Ruby on Rails SaaS codebases

- You need to have some design knowledge to adjust things manually, you need to ask for exactly what you want, in the technical jargon it expects. You can't just say "make this more beautiful" or "animate this better" because it just creates slop

- Right now vibe coded videos are promising, but I think I could have done this video faster just by doing it manually in After Effects. It really took that much work

- If you have a creative idea for something you want to animate, it takes multiple hours of back and forth prompting to create just one or two seconds worth of **good** animation

- Tip: PARAMETERIZE everything! It tends to hardcode magic numbers everywhere in the code, so if you change something earlier in the video timeline, everything else breaks. You want to essentially be creating "key frames" with code by telling it to parameterize every frame where something important happens, and calculate the rest of the keyframes based off that. This comes in handy when you need, for example, to adjust keyframes to match the music

So in summary: vibe coded videos are promising, but right now it only works for very stock-looking videos unless you put in a ton of effort

Maybe actually useful for 1-2 second web animations though, I'll try that next

It will obviously get better, this feels like the quality of code generation in 2023-2024, you need to hold its hand and correct it at every step along the way. But even if video code generation was better, you would still need someone with motion design knowledge to at least set the creative direction, lay out the overall script and composition, etc. It's not completely hands-off unless you want slop

And a word on caution: especially here on X, there's 90% hype and 10% reality, nothing is what it seems. Do not believe what you see online, people are constantly baiting and then just laughing it off in the comments

Claude Code tip: install huashu-art-motion and Opus 5.5 can draw animations in 𝟯𝟱 𝗮𝗿𝘁 𝘀𝘁𝘆𝗹𝗲𝘀 with code. Van Gogh's starry sky swirls. Dalí's clocks drip. And its delivery script rejects any film where almost nothing moves.

You can just ask for an animation in the style of Van Gogh, Monet or Bauhaus, an explainer animation to go with your voiceover, or a character walking through one famous painting after another. Hand it a reference animation and it first breaks down the cuts, the beat and what moves where in the frame, then recreates it in code.

𝗪𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻 𝟭𝟬 𝗺𝗶𝗻𝘂𝘁𝗲𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝗶𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝘁, Opus 5.5 made this demo video from its 35 built-in styles. It runs from cave painting 40,000 years ago all the way to 2026. The room, the cat and the girl never change; only the style does.

17 that work for any subject: products, data, stories
→ Van Gogh, Matisse cut-outs, Seurat pointillism, Impressionism
→ Analytic Cubism, Lichtenstein pop art, Bauhaus, Russian Constructivism
→ Ghibli watercolor backgrounds, Makoto Shinkai light, Chinese ink wash
→ 8-bit pixel art, vaporwave neon, 2026 flat illustration
→ Pompeii mosaic, early ray-traced CGI, Rembrandt chiaroscuro

18 for time travel, tributes and art-history speedruns
→ Monet's water lilies, Klimt's golden period, Munch, Dalí
→ Hopper, Picasso's blue period, Mucha's Art Nouveau
→ Keith Haring, Kusama polka dots, Jack Kirby comics, 1930s rubber hose cartoons
→ Cave painting, Egyptian tomb murals, Greek black-figure pottery, Dunhuang murals
→ Chinese shadow puppets, Gothic illuminated manuscripts, Renaissance sfumato

Each style spells out what moves in the picture. The eyes on Klimt's robe blink in turn, Hopper's hard-edged patch of sunlight slides slowly across a face, and the 8-bit question block pops out a coin.

9 explainer styles
→ For math and AI concepts, use 3Blue1Brown, where one shape morphs into the next
→ For data, use finance charts: axes first, then the data, and label only one thing
→ For UI steps in a software tutorial, use the keynote look: light-spot background, frosted-glass cards, big numbers
→ To draw relationships as you narrate, use the whiteboard, where the pen tip reveals the line art bit by bit
→ For a collage of graphics and info, use the Vox explainer look: clippings, red lines, highlighter
→ Kurzgesagt, flat with no outlines, moving between tiny and huge scales
→ Storytime, cutting to reaction close-ups and leaving a beat for the joke
→ Kinetic type, with the key word slamming into the frame
→ Presenter-led finance explainers, where you supply the character yourself

The music is synthesized in code too, note by note on a BPM grid. When a film is done, it runs its QA script, then sends an agent that took no part in making it to watch only the finished film and find problems. The delivery script also blocks two more things: 0.3+ seconds of blank frames mid-film, and a blue-purple background in over 30% of the film, a palette it counts as AI slop.

The skill has 𝗮 𝘁𝗶𝗲𝗿 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗖𝗹𝗮𝘂𝗱𝗲 𝗢𝗽𝘂𝘀 𝟱.𝟱 or stronger models, where it can combine the libraries itself and write its own renderers. All 35 styles are star-rated, and the 20 with three stars are recognizable at a glance and ready to use.

The skill's docs are in Chinese; the prompt below has it read them and talk to you in English.
Rendering video needs uv, ffmpeg and Playwright Chromium.
If you want people on screen, use your own character art or connect an image model to make the frames. Without either, it only draws hands and figures seen from behind.

npx skills add alchaincyf/huashu-art-motion
https://t.co/tGUVjIj4FB

Once it's installed, send this to Opus 5.5 in Claude Code 👇

"Use huashu-art-motion to make me a 15-second animation. The skill's docs are in Chinese; read them and talk to me in English.
1. First check for uv, ffmpeg and Playwright Chromium, and tell me how to install anything that's missing.
2. Ask me what it's about, who it's for, and whether it's landscape or portrait. From the material layer in references/风格配方/INDEX.md, pick 3 styles that fit, three-star ones first. Redesign the composition for my subject in all three, each different from the others, and don't copy the room from the samples. Show me one still frame of each to choose from.
3. Once I pick, give each scene one main action plus two motif loops from that style's card. For Van Gogh, that's the starry sky curling into swirls and the lamp's halo spreading outward. If there's music, use the skill's BPM synthesis and put the motion on the beat.
4. If people need to appear, ask me first: my own character art, frames from an image model, or only hands and figures seen from behind.
5. After rendering, follow the skill's own QA steps: run its QA script first, then send a subagent that took no part in making it to watch only the finished film and find problems, have it write its findings into the 审片/ folder, and deliver with its delivery script. If anything comes up red, fix it and re-render before giving it to me."

Introducing Reel Farmer

Paste a YouTube URL, get TikTok/Reel with animated captions in one command. Fully local.

> How it works:

1. yt-dlp downloads the video
2. LLM reads the transcript and picks the most clip-worthy moments
3. FFmpeg cuts each clip, silence removed automatically
4. Whisper.cpp runs locally for word-level timestamps
5. Remotion renders animated captions
6. Combines everything into 1080x1920 reels

Every stage checkpoints to SQLite. In case of a crash, it'll pick up exactly where it left off.
